articles.title_orig: In China’s tech mecca, Trump and Xi touted AI cooperation. Now comes the harsh reality.
articles.title_zh: In China’s tech mecca, Trump and Xi touted AI cooperation. Now comes the harsh reality.
articles.content_orig:
For Chinese leader Xi Jinping, hosting US President Donald Trump in the futuristic city of Shenzhen was a chance to show just how far the nation’s high-tech industry has come.
But neither Trump nor Xi seemed keen to address an unpleasant reality – that the US had just announced fresh efforts to keep it from advancing much further, amid allegations a Chinese intelligence operation had targeted the head of Nvidia, one of America’s most important tech companies.
The two heads of state met for the third time this year during an annual gathering of economic leaders from the Asia-Pacific region. Like the last two times, the meeting itself was a sign of reassurance for what has become a bitter and bruising rivalry.
Amid all the grand gestures, including a historic meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia, neither side was willing to dredge up the scandal threatening a delicate detente between the world’s two largest economies.
Allegations that Jensen Huang, who until recently helmed the $4 trillion chip titan Nvidia, was having an affair with a woman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, have reignited fears of America’s best technology falling into adversarial hands.
Then, two days before Trump landed in Shenzhen, the Commerce Department issued new licensing requirements aimed at further cutting off Chinese access to advanced US chips.
“With the fallout of Nvidia and these new export control rules landing just before the summit, I think the uneasy truce between the US and China is even more fragile,” said Benjamin Kostrzewa, an international trade law expert and Hong Kong-based partner at the law firm Hogan Lovells Cadwalader.
In a carefully orchestrated week of events for corporate executives and global delegates, Xi’s priority was to portray China as a reliable and innovative economic partner that welcomed foreign businesses. But analysts said America’s latest chip curbs, likely seen as an escalation of US protectionist policies, would be hard for Beijing to ignore much longer.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the new restrictions “a typical case of economic coercion.” The day before Xi greeted Trump warmly at the foot of Air Force One, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce warned: “If the US insists on this direction, China will take countermeasures and firmly safeguard its national sovereignty, security and development interests.”
A tentative economic ceasefire between the US and China was already on shaky ground.
When Trump and Xi last convened in Washington, DC in September, they extended a trade agreement from October 2025, which included a rollback of US tariffs in exchange for Chinese commitments to buy more US agricultural products and loosen restrictions on rare earth exports.
Officials said the two-month extension, set to expire January 10, would allow them to assess whether China could alleviate US concerns that it was coming up short on its original pledges.
Now the controversy over Nvidia – and how some of its most advanced chips reach China despite US export controls – has triggered greater suspicion over national security risks that will complicate negotiations, said Jyh-An Lee, law professor and executive director of the Centre for Legal Innovation and Digital Society at The Chinese University of Hong Kong.
“The political climate is now quite different,” Lee said. “It’s not that easy to go back to the time before the Jensen Huang incident.”
At the summit, the US, China and Russia said they discussed the need to develop artificial intelligence safely. Otherwise, there was little concrete progress on trade or technological cooperation.
In a Wednesday interview with Fox News, Trump said he raised Huang briefly with Xi, only to lament the “tragedy” of the Nvidia co-founder stepping down. Chinese officials have decried allegations that Beijing was using Huang’s affair to obtain sensitive information as baseless attempts to smear China.
Semiconductors have become a major flashpoint in the US-China relationship, as each nation has invested heavily in surpassing the other in AI and advanced technological capabilities. While China has made it a national priority to be able to develop its own semiconductors, many of its tech companies still use American chips.
That fierce rivalry will make it hard for the two nations to collaborate on sensitive sectors like technology, even as leaders tout dialogue on AI safety. And Huang’s resignation means the loss of one of the most vocal advocates for selling more US chips to China.
“The US has been trying to find more bargaining chips, and I think chips might be the most valuable asset that US still has the advantage over,” said Lee.
As the host of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, it was in Xi’s best interest to maintain an image of openness and collaboration during the summit.
“Simply the optics of China hosting APEC puts him in a really powerful position, so in many ways he comes out as a winner,” said Han Lin, China country director for The Asia Group, a business consulting firm. “That said, China has to retaliate. They have no choice.”
Still, Lin said China would likely take subtle actions to try and preserve stability ahead of the politically important Communist Party Congress next year, at which Xi is expected to claim another five-year term as leader.
One of the most effective countermeasures at China’s disposal is its near-monopoly on rare earths and other minerals critical to many high-tech supply chains. Despite the trade agreement reached last year, Chinese rare earth exports to the US remain about 75% below pre-restriction levels, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“China can hit back, and they can hit back hard,” said Lin. “They still continue to have the critical earth minerals export control leverage, and that really is the leverage for all seasons.”
Analysts said as US lawmakers increase scrutiny over tech exports to China, that will likely lead to stronger enforcement of existing regulations, as well as new rules.
Trump and Xi are set to meet once more this year, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit in December. But in January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after their sweeping midterm election victory, which could put pressure on Trump in his dealings with Xi.
Holding the majority would allow opponents to push back on Trump’s more aggressive protectionist policies, giving China more leverage to negotiate next year. But Democrats have also called for stronger tech export controls in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, and voiced concerns about the threat that Chinese tech poses to US national security.
“The takeaway we’ve been telling our US clients has been, if you have any ask of the Chinese government, better you ask sooner than later,” Lin said. “You have one final chance in G20. After which, well, we’re going to be playing a different game going forward.”

articles.title_orig: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a mistake
articles.title_zh: Poland says Russian missiles hit its territory; Trump calls it a mistake
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Fossil fuel dispute threatens to derail COP31 climate deal
articles.title_zh: Fossil fuel dispute threatens to derail COP31 climate deal
articles.content_orig:
Will COP31 end with a new global climate deal?
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.
Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
And it includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
Countries were expected to reconvene at 09:00 local time (06:00GMT) to decide whether to approve a new deal.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President Murat Kurum says he believes the third version of the text sent to delegates addresses outlying concerns.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said.  "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
Panama's Minister of Environment Juan Carlos Navarro says it is not acceptable for a COP agreement not to mention fossil fuels.
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
In the latest text the commitments to CCUS have been reduced, which may be enough to alleviate the EU's concerns.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, says the summit should focus on the shift towards clean energy.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
One of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money - appears unresolved in the latest draft agreement.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (Â£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

articles.title_orig: What to Do Now to Prepare for the Next Bank Outage
articles.title_zh: What to Do Now to Prepare for the Next Bank Outage
articles.content_orig:
Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com .
Other banks that saw a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts included Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.
However, Downdetector showed that service was back to normal at the banks and Zelle early Tuesday.
CBS News has reached out for comment to Chase, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Capital One.
Bank of America told CBS News in a statement that its "systems were operating normally throughout the day yesterday."
Chase Bank's services were experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."
Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."
Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank.
Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector.
Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the outage tracker. A Bank of America spokesperson told CBS News its "systems have been operating normally today."
U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation.
A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News.
A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally.
Zelle told CBS News its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments.
"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.
The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights. The FAA said Sunday that airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal . (On Monday evening, United Airlines also said it resolved a " widespread system outage " it had been dealing with that afternoon.)
Cybersecurity experts said the root causes of the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem.
"Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day."
He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide.
"We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added.
When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University.
"The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected."
Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on site when online banking resources go down.
"Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," he said in a statement to CBS News.
He also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions.
"Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said.
He also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said.
Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial-crime organization, told CBS News he expects criminals to exploit consumer anxiety about potentially losing access to their money, and that consumers should "assume they will be targeted." That's in part because AI lets scammers act fast and at scale.
Timm said common tactics to be alert to include criminals exerting pressure on targets "to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access."
"These scams may take the form of fake bank alerts, phishing texts or emails, or social media posts that claim to offer help," he said. "Some schemes aim to steal banking login credentials, while others use malicious links to gain access to a victim's computer."
Edited by Alain  Sherter and Aimee  Picchi
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Naughty Dog Dev Says GTA 6 Is Like a 'Bugatti Veyron to a Nervous Victorian Child'
articles.title_zh: Naughty Dog Dev Says GTA 6 Is Like a 'Bugatti Veyron to a Nervous Victorian Child'
articles.content_orig:
Naughty Dog’s Michael Barclay – whose credits include Uncharted: The Lost Legacy and The Last of Us 2 – says he’s “made video games for 19 years and GTA 6 appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child”.
Rockstar’s latest open world release is by far the best-looking game ever made, even if it is locked to 30fps on PS5 hardware .
And it’s being treated like witchcraft by devs, who naturally have a greater appreciation for the feats on display.
Barclay, who’s currently working on next year’s Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet , continued :
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
“I'm always astonished that [Rockstar’s] environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting.”
In really, really simple terms, baked lighting is a game development technique used to save computational cost by calculating light and shadow data in advance.
The downside to this is that it’s fixed, but obviously given the ever-changing nature of GTA 6’s sandbox, it needs to have a dynamic solution.
Barclay is saying that GTA 6’s dynamic lighting matches and even surpasses those pre-determined solutions in many scenarios, making it a real accomplishment.
These comments triggered discussion from various other industry professionals, including Tim Soret from Odd Tales, the makers of The Last Night , who outlined some of his thoughts on the title:
GTA 6 sets a standard so unfathomably high I do wonder at what point it’ll ever be topped.
I suppose raising the bar like this will motivate the many other talented devs around the world, but not every studio will have access to the time and the estimated $1 billion budget that allowed Rockstar to deliver this.
Either way, it’s clear industry professionals are utterly blown away by what the studio has delivered here.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

articles.title_orig: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
articles.title_zh: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
articles.content_orig:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?
So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.
It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training -  those dubbed as Neets - this week.
Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".
The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.
But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?
Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.
But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".
He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not.
"I've spent all that time and energy submitting my application but got nothing in return."
Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.
The 24-year-old says her biggest challenge throughout the job-hunting process has been not getting feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.
She says she has also been ghosted after interviews several times.
"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.
Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.
The Milburn report says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.
"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, a 21-year-old, from Swindon.
Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.
And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.
But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.
Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.
"It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.
The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.
But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?
Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.
"If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong... You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is."
There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds.
Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.
"Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate. Put it down to experience and move on."

articles.title_orig: China’s $1.7 Trillion AI Rout Turns Hot Trade Into Losing Bet
articles.title_zh: China’s $1.7 Trillion AI Rout Turns Hot Trade Into Losing Bet
articles.content_orig:
U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.
China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.
That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni said in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his plan to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.
Real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.
With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.
But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.
“To keep AI funding flowing, Xi needs a buoyant stock market,” the note said. “Otherwise, AI risks being folded into the state-owned enterprise (SOE) universe that his team has pledged to shrink since 2013, further crowding out the private sector.”
Retail investors are also skittish about Chinese stocks after Xi’s government cracked down on the tech sector in 2020. The market’s reputation as a rigged casino that favors politically connected insiders doesn’t help either. In fact, the Shanghai Composite remains well below its October 2007 peak despite China’s GDP exploding nearly sixfold.
Many households now have “financial PTSD” after repeated stock busts, including a crash in the summer of 2015 that required an aggressive national team rescue, Yardeni added.
To be sure, China remains a leader in AI, and mom-and-pop investors still drive most of the trade, even as they treat the market more like high-stakes gambling than a place to grow retirement savings.
“Yet this is a moment of real danger for Xi. A bursting AI bubble would not merely erase wealth or dent China’s technological prestige. It would weaken Beijing’s attempt to replace a broken property model with a stock-market-led one,” Yardeni warned.
“China can build world-class AI models, train engineers, and spend billions on chips. But if its households still view Shanghai as a casino with odds set by the Politburo, Xi’s dream of creating a Chinese version of Wall Street may remain just that: a dream.”
Underscoring its importance to Beijing, Premier Li Qiang told a State Council executive meeting earlier this month that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the rest of the year.
It followed securities regulators sharply easing requirements for company buybacks that help lift stock prices and discouraging IPOs and large share sales to prevent stock dilution that triggers selloffs.
But the spy scandal that dethroned Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia represents a new risk to China’s AI ambitions. Backlash over the advanced U.S. chips and computing capacity that China had access to has spurred the Trump administration to impose new technology curbs.
“By targeting both indirect chip shipments to China and its access to overseas computing power, the new controls threaten to slow the catch-up of China’s leading AI models and to slow China’s AI rollout,” analysts at Capital Economics wrote on Tuesday.
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Intel Nova Lake-H Spec Sheet Shows Up With a 4.8 GHz Boost and 25 W TDP
articles.title_zh: Intel Nova Lake-H Spec Sheet Shows Up With a 4.8 GHz Boost and 25 W TDP
articles.content_orig:
We finally got a glimpse of one of the upcoming 16-core Nova Lake mobile chip, and what it brings to the table.
Here is one of the early appearances of one of the upcoming Intel Core Ultra 4 series processors. Thanks to @momomo_us, we got a glimpse of a Nova Lake-H mobile processor on an Advantech board (for robotics and industrial applications), which is going to power the next-gen mainstream mobile devices. The specs sheet doesn't mention the SKU model name, but it mentions "Core Ultra Series 4" and "Nova Lake-H" as the codename.
The specs sheet details most of its specifications, including the core configuration, cache size, memory support, and TDP rating. The processor uses an 8P+4E+4LPE configuration, combining eight performance cores, four efficient cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Even though this is the same configuration as the 16-core Nova Lake-S processor we reported on previously , this one is specifically for the mobile platform.
The processor is expected to carry the Coyote Cove architecture for the P cores and Arctic Wolf E cores as previously reported. The 16-core Nova Lake-H leaked SKU is reportedly featuring a good 4.8 GHz Turbo clock, 2.0 GHz base clock, and 18 MB of LLC cache. The page also mentions its integrated graphics configuration, which reportedly features a 2.3 GHz clock speed. However, details like execution units and architecture are missing.
It's expected that the Nova Lake-H SKUs will have integrated Arc graphics based on the Xe3P architecture and will carry up to 12 GPU cores for the higher-end variants. This might be the one that carries the 12-GPU-core configuration, but we will wait for official confirmation. One more interesting detail here is the memory support. The processor reportedly supports DDR5-8000 MT/s and up to 128 GB of capacity. This aligns with our previous reports that suggested a good 800 MT/s jump over Panther Lake, which supports DDR5-7200 MT/s.
Another key detail is the power rating, as the leaked specs reveal the SKU reportedly runs at a 25W TDP. This is well below the power range expected from the Nova Lake-S desktop processors, for which vendors have started introducing PSUs with three 8-pin EPS connectors .
The leaker @momomo_us also spotted a Nova Lake-S listing on the OpenBenchmarking platform. This is an early Nova Lake-S sample with 28 Cores and up to 5.2 GHz turbo boost. This is likely the 8P+16E+4LP-E configuration chip that could carry a 296W PL2 limit .

articles.title_orig: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
articles.title_zh: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump on Friday signed the Common Cents Act , which lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law.
It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents. For example, if a purchase costs $10.02 after tax and a customer is short 2 cents, the tab would round down to $10 under the act. A charge of $10.04 would round up to $10.05.
Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor.
Business advocacy groups cheered its passage. NACS, which represents the convenience and fuel retailing industry, said it creates reliable guidelines for conducting cash transactions.
"Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended," Brennan Duckett, NACS' director of regulatory and policy, said in a statement to CBS News. "NACS members benefit directly from this law, and we are pleased to see President Trump make it official with his signature."
Business owners said they faced confusion and were vulnerable to litigation before the act passed.
"As a retailer, I am grateful to have established legal guidance on rounding cash transactions," Scott Zietlow, CEO and president of Kwik Trip, said in a statement Friday. "Every cash transaction that we processed in recent months was a reminder that we needed more clarity from the federal government. We've now got that clarity."

articles.title_orig: At least 24 dead in Nigeria when boat capsizes while carrying people to a funeral - ABC News
articles.title_zh: At least 24 dead in Nigeria when boat capsizes while carrying people to a funeral - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to be on board.
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A boat carrying people to a funeral has capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, emergency services said on Saturday.
The boat was taking passengers from one community to another for a burial ceremony when it sank on Friday in Bayelsa State in the country’s South South region, Nigeria’s National Emergency Management Agency spokesman Manzo Ezeki said in a statement.
He said that search and rescue operations were ongoing without specifying how many people were missing.
Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said on Friday that another 24 people had been rescued and sought medical assistance.
Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to have been on board.
Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer toward land, but he allegedly declined, according to Mohammed. The boat operator then reportedly fled the scene, while the manager of the boat was taken into custody.
The Bayelsa state government responded by urging boat operators and passengers to adhere to safety regulations.
“Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life,” Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Boat tragedies are common in Nigeria. A lack of enforcement of safety regulations means faulty boats without life jackets sometimes operate in the country.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
articles.title_zh: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates , hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers . The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push . Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."
Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.
"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley posted on X on Saturday.
Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_orig: Challenge accepted: meet the *non-hybrid* 670bhp Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale
articles.title_zh: Challenge accepted: meet the *non-hybrid* 670bhp Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale
articles.content_orig:
And it's not a limited-production rarity either. Welcome to the coolest 296 yet
Lighter, harder, faster, noisier, wingier. And no hybrid. Just when you thought this was a regular approach to making a Ferrari go faster, in comes that final nugget.
The 296 Challenge Stradale is combustion only. Ferrari has stripped out the electric motors and battery, reducing weight by 140kg and power by nearly 200bhp.
There’s a lot going on here. Traditionally Ferrari only builds one special version of its mid-engined cars. But this is the second derivative of the standard 296 GTB . Last year we had the 868bhp Speciale , now we have the 670bhp Challenge Stradale.
And there’s more good news: this isn’t a limited edition model only being made available to a handful of Ferrari’s best collectors. It’s a full production model. And - relatively speaking of course - it’s going to be a bargain, priced almost exactly in line with the entry-level 296 GTB at around £260,000. A return to the good old days where the stripped out car was the cheap one.
And it has been stripped out. It’s been released alongside (and developed with) a newly enhanced 296 race car, the Challenge Evo, used for one-make racing. Outwardly the most obvious differences are the wing mirrors and plexiglass windows.
Neither is pretty. The soft elegant curves of the 296 GTB have been lost, hidden behind all manner of bolt-on winglets, vents, flicks and foils. The rear wing is a thumper, alone responsible for 270kg of downforce.
For a car that has a claimed performance balance of ’80 per cent road, 20 per cent track’ it’s a bit OTT. Elegance has been sacrificed on the altar of aero.
Total downforce is 617kg at 155mph. At the same speed Porsche’s GT3 RS is rumoured to develop around 640kg. They weigh about the same too. Porsche quotes a 1,450kg wet weight, Ferrari a 1,330kg dry weight.
But here’s something different. Ferrari has managed to keep the front boot, where Porsche hasn’t. Admittedly it’s half the size it used to be, just 67 litres, a narrow gutter flanked by air channels that bring hot air from the rads up through the bonnet. I wouldn’t go putting the gelato in there for long. But it’s there, which signals Ferrari appreciates this car has to be usable, something it forgot to its cost with the luggage-less SF90.
Removing the hybrid has meant lots of engine tweaking. From fattening up the torque curve at the bottom to enhancing the power delivery up above 8,000rpm. The Challenge Stradale uses the Speciale’s engine, complete with titanium conrods and nitrided steel crankshaft, but power has been lifted 7bhp to 670bhp.
Get all the latest news, reviews and exclusives, direct to your inbox.
That’s the same power as the 488 back in 2015, but from an engine two cylinders and one litre smaller.
It should sound good too. The new exhaust promises to enhance harmonics and the 296's sound tube, bringing noise back to the cabin, has been recalibrated. As fierce and strident as the GT3 RS’s nat asp flat six? Let’s not get carried away.
It will be faster than the Porsche. The promise is 62mph in 2.8secs, 124mph in 7.9secs. The Porsche’s times are 3.2 and 10.6. As far as sibling rivalry goes, it matches the 296 Speciale to the first marker, lags a second getting to the latter. Around tracks it’s a different story. “At Fiorano and other twistier tracks the Challenge Stradale is faster,” claims Matteo Turconi, the Challenge Stradale’s senior product manager, “at high speed circuits like Monza, the Speciale is faster.”
Fortunately, Magneride is capable of minor miracles
The most radical change to the suspension was to the springs - the main spring is now almost twice as stiff, so Ferrari has added a softer helper spring - a solution carried straight over from the Evo race car.
The damping is still done with the adaptive Magneride system, but for the first time ever on a Ferrari there are actually two bumpy road settings rather than one. What we can deduce from this is that the ride quality is… uncompromising. Fortunately, Magneride is capable of minor miracles.
There are carbon ceramic brakes, you can have the carbon wheels as an option (saving 2kg per corner) and track widths are up a little (13mm front, 22mm rear), just helping to pack out the arches and deliver a little bit more lateral grip.
According to Turconi, “this is not a car for everyone. If you want to slide, you don’t want this car. This is like going back 30 years, it’s more precise, more challenging, with less assistance. It’s more difficult to drive. The brake pedal is firmer and has less travel, the throttle spring is stiffer and the steering is heavier”.
You guess as much the moment you get in. The carbon door panels have some shape, but no material covering, likewise the centre console. You sit lower on carbon race seats borrowed from the F80 - lesser chairs are available. Nor do you have to have race harnesses.
Sound deadening has been stripped as part of all the weight saving, but there are some things even Ferrari can’t dodge - the hardcore Challenge Stradale still has adaptive cruise, lane keep, sign recognition and driver drowsiness detection. Shouldn’t be any need for the last one. Or the others come to think of it.
Ferrari can be trusted to make it a blistering driver’s car. Fair play to them for not making it a limited edition special and charging the earth for it. But more than that it signals a diversification at Ferrari. And it looks like they’ve been taking lessons from Porsche’s 911.
This one, we have a feeling, will help steady the ship
The Speciale now seems to be positioned akin to the 911 Turbo - the same basic experience as the standard car, just enhanced, more power, luxury and usability. In this narrative the Challenge Stradale tracks the GT3's more closely. It’s sensible thinking - Porsche GT cars are much less powerful than the Turbos, but it’s never held them back, they are rawer, more exciting.
The timing is interesting too. 2026 has been a torrid year for Maranello. It gave us the Luce . It got kicked in the plums. The Dodici Cilindri Manuale was meant to take the pain away, only for people to turn around and complain it’s not a proper manual. It’s well known that the 296 hasn’t been selling well. So the Challenge Stradale follows hot on the heels of the Speciale.
This one, we have a feeling, will help steady the ship.

articles.title_orig: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
articles.title_zh: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
articles.content_orig:
Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.
Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.
Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act . The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.
Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.
Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin , and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

articles.title_orig: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
articles.title_zh: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
articles.content_orig:
Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.
That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

articles.title_orig: Iran launches attacks in Bahrain, Hormuz and moves against US blockade
articles.title_zh: Iran launches attacks in Bahrain, Hormuz and moves against US blockade
articles.content_orig:
Iran launched two waves of drone and ballistic missile attacks on Saturday night against four US bases in Bahrain, home to the US’ Fifth Fleet headquarters, the Iranian media reported, while Bahrain announced the attacks, warning the population to shelter.
Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency claimed that the Iranian military targeted four US bases in Bahrain, with two of the named as Sheikh Isa and Juffair, in what it called a response to continued US incursions in Iran’s airspace.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed that it struck 2 Patriot defence batteries and a radar system. Bahrain and the US military did not confirm the claims.
Bahrain said that its air defence intercepted several Iranian attacks, calling them a “heinous Iranian aggression”.
Local sources in Bahrain reported loud explosions and Bahrain’s Interior ministry announced that a fire broke out at a civilian industrial compound, with no injuries reported, while local videos showed smoke rising from a fire in an unidentified location.
Right after the attack on Bahrain, reports emerged from southern Iran of explosions in Sirik. The US military has retaliated regularly against Iranian military facilities in recent weeks.
Earlier on Saturday, US Central Command CENTCOM denied Iranian claims that a surface-to-air missile damaged a US F-16 fighter jet on Friday evening.
Meanwhile, at least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.
In a sharp increase of incidents in the Strait of Hormuz over the last week, the UK military’s maritime security center (UKMTO) said two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. There were no reports of casualties.
The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait and caught fire. State media also said that the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels.
Iran’s army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia warned the US again on Saturday that any attack on Iran will be met with “a decisive and immediate response” as “we are much stronger than in the past,” Iranian TV IRIB report.
“Any new aggression will be met with a decisive, immediate and effective response from the armed forces, and the defence of the country will not be limited to a specific geographical area,” Akraminia said during a visit to Iranian troops in the south of the country.
The Iranian TV showed for the first time the ground troops deployed into defensive positions in the coastal areas of southern Iran on Saturday.
Meanwhile on Saturday, as more than 14 Iranian tankers are reported to be prepared off Kharg Island to break out of the US military blockade in the coming days, Iran’s deputy minister of foreign affairs Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that the US blockade of Iranian ports “is an act of war and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege.”
Iran warned of a “fierce military response” if the convoy was engaged by the US military, threatening with widespread attacks on energy infrastructures across the Gulf region.
Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian also said that Iran is subject to a “silent economic war” which is “tougher than a war with missiles,” adding that Iran has the capability to withstand it.
As Gharibabadi announced that Tehran has warned the United States that the Iranian convoy will sail soon to China, the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War said that “Iranian attempts to run the blockade impose a series of dilemmas on the United States by either collapsing the blockade or returning to a war that imposes unideal political costs on the United States by straining its relationships with Gulf allies.”
Against the backdrop of the intensifying crisis, the diplomatic negotiations between the US and Iran spearheaded by Qatar continue.
Iran’s deputy foreign minister Gharibabadi announced on Saturday that a Qatari delegation held talks with Iranian officials on Friday evening for some two hours, before returning to Doha.
Iranian Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi suggested that a deal is possible when he declared that reopening the Strait of Hormuz would be “not difficult” if the US accepted Iran’s “reasonable conditions,” especially by ending the blockade which he called “completely illegal,” lifting sanctions and Washington acknowledging “past mistakes.”
In parallel, US president Donald Trump told US network Fox News on Saturday that he planned to make a “permanent” deal with Iran to prevent it from acquiring a nuclear weapon and that he was never interested in a regime change in Iran.
“I intend to reach a permanent deal with Iran that prevents them from obtaining nuclear weapons, even if another president takes my place in the future and is unfit for the office,” Trump said.

articles.title_orig: Bahrain says Iranian attack hits industrial facility as air defences intercept attacks
articles.title_zh: Bahrain says Iranian attack hits industrial facility as air defences intercept attacks
articles.content_orig:
Iran targeted a Kuwaiti air base that hosts US forces on Wednesday, widening the scope of its attacks after the US military hit what it said was a missile launch site in Iran.
Iran’s army targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait with drones, state-run Press TV reported. The Kuwaiti Army’s General Staff said any explosions heard were caused by air defense systems intercepting incoming attacks.
Neighboring Bahrain, which is home to the US Fifth Fleet and has faced repeated Iranian attacks over the past week, also sounded air raid sirens early Wednesday, with the military saying it had intercepted “a number of Iranian aerial attacks” early Wednesday.
CNN has contacted the US Central Command (CENTCOM) for comment.
Just hours earlier, US fighter jets carried out a “self-defense” strike against an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island using “precision munitions,” according to an American military official.
The strike “was in response to IRGC aggression targeting American personnel and assets,” the official said, noting that CENTCOM remains “highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region.”
Iranian state media reported that an area on the outskirts of a city on Qeshm Island had been targeted in an “enemy attack.” Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan province for political and security affairs, said the strike caused no damage to vital infrastructure, commercial or residential areas.
Iran’s widening attacks come as Tehran warns it will not accept a prolonged stalemate in its war with the US, while President Donald Trump has signaled a preference for maintaining crippling economic pressure on the Islamic Republic rather than resuming full-scale hostilities. Iran has also threatened to expand the war significantly and warned that it will not wait for another US attack before striking.
Tuesday’s US strikes appear similar to others in recent weeks around the Strait of Hormuz, which US officials have also characterized as defensive, rather than marking a significant escalation by American forces.
A third US aircraft carrier strike group recently entered CENTCOM’s area of responsibility, where it is expected to — at least temporarily — join ongoing operations that include enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and conducting escort operations for commercial ships willing to transit the Strait.
Attacks on oil and gas tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have surged in recent weeks. On Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates’ state-owned ADNOC energy company said one of its vessels had been attacked while transiting the waterway the previous evening, leaving 11 crew members injured and one missing.
“Today’s developments should serve as an important reminder of the inherent instability of the current situation,” Hamidreza Azizi, an Iran analyst at Crisis Group, wrote on X. “Some within the Trump administration – and perhaps even Trump himself – may believe that Washington can maintain economic pressure and the naval blockade against Iran indefinitely while avoiding another full-scale war. But the developments of the past 24 hours demonstrate how difficult it is to sustain such an arrangement.”
There is little indication of an imminent diplomatic agreement to end the conflict, and Trump has warned he could resume full combat operations if Tehran refuses to accept the US administration’s demands.
Trump was widely expected to hold off on restarting those combat operations until after the US midterm elections but appears to still be mulling over how to proceed, absent a last-minute deal.
With Democrats poised to take control of the House and Senate in January, Trump’s window to decide on a path forward in Iran appears to be shrinking. CNN has previously reported that it is likely untenable for the US military to maintain the status quo indefinitely, but only Trump has the power to decide when the war is over.
CNN’s Abbas Al Lawati, Lucas Lilieholm and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
articles.content_orig:
Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro is in intensive care after being diagnosed with an acute bowel obstruction, according to the DF Star hospital where he is being treated.
Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted on Friday with abdominal pain. In a bulletin on Saturday, the hospital said doctors have started giving him fluids and nutritional support, and inserted a tube into his stomach.
It said the former president is clinically stable and conscious, although they said there was no projected date for his discharge.
“There is hope that his condition will improve,” his son, Senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro, wrote on X on Saturday afternoon. “He is being closely monitored and is fighting to get his bowels working again, with his usual grit and focus.”
In the early hours of Saturday morning, he described his father’s difficult night of treatment, where food residue was removed from his stomach using a tube inserted into his nose, and bouts of nausea.
“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote, suggesting that his father might need another surgery, which would be his 10th in less than eight years.
“All this is happening to a man sentenced to 27 years in prison without having committed any crime, while criminals do whatever they want with what’s left of this country,” the younger Bolsonaro continued.
Bolsonaro has been serving a 27-year sentence since last year for an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro has denied the charges.
He has been hospitalised repeatedly and has had to undergo surgeries after being stabbed in 2018 during a campaign event.
He was transferred in March to house arrest after spending several months in jail because of his health issues.
Next month, Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to consider the constitutionality of a law that changes how sentences are calculated, which could shorten his sentence and those of others convicted in the 2022 coup plot.

articles.title_orig: Russian cargo ship ablaze in Baltic Sea after drone strike, crew evacuates
articles.title_zh: Russian cargo ship ablaze in Baltic Sea after drone strike, crew evacuates
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.content_orig:

Vladimir Putinâs crusade to win over war veterans has been brutally exposed as a farce by members of his own party.
The Russian leaderâs âTime of Heroesâ program has, since its inception in early 2024, sought to put a romanticized spin on the Kremlinâs war against Ukraine and the meat grinder tactics used by the military to keep feeding the war machine, signaling to both military veterans and the wider Russian public that those who have served on the battlefield will serve as the countryâs new âeliteâ and hold prestigious places in government.
That notion went up in flames this week after two local lawmakers from Putinâs United Russia party were caught using their supposed enthusiasm for the program to lure vulnerable men into a deranged scheme. After forcing the men to sign contracts to join the war, they arranged quick marriages before deployment and set up bank accounts to receive âdeath benefitsâ for their newlywed husbandsâ inevitable battlefield demise.
Irina Bezman showed off her new husband in a social media post nodding to the "time of heroes."
Federal investigators in Krasnoyarsk Krai detailed the bizarre plot in a press release announcing the chargesâthough they neglected to mention that two of the suspects were the face of Putinâs local âTime of Heroesâ program as deputies of United Russia.
The group first stole a one-time payment issued to one of the men for his military service in the amount of 1.8 million rubles ($22,000), and âfollowing the death of the service member, the group stole another 5 million rubles from his bank account,â investigators said.
They reportedly failed to get access to the bank account of the other duped groom.
The two women, identified in local reports as 41-year-old Irina Bezman and 64-year-old Galina Kalimulina, worked as deputies of the Sharypovo District Council and routinely posted about their support for the war.
It was one of their social media posts that reportedly triggered local scrutiny: Bezman, in a now-deleted post, shared a photo of herself with her new husband, Vladimir, holding up their marriage certificate at the local registration office.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (C), Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev (L) and Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu (R) attend a wreath laying ceremony at the tomb of the unknown soldier to mark the Defender of the Fatheland Day on February 23, 2015 in central Moscow, Russia.
Sasha Mordovets/Getty Images
The local outlet Zapad24 reports that residents were immediately baffled to see the local councilwoman had married a man from a very different walk of life, known mainly for hanging out on a local churchâs steps and sweeping the courtyard.
Kalimulina, who had served as the executive secretary of the regional branch of United Russia, was described as the mastermind of the scheme.
She filled her social media pages with posts in support of the war and Russian troops, often signing off on them with the hashtag âWe donât abandon our own.â
