articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran; warns next move may not come until 2027
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday offered unusually warm praise for the top two Democrats in Congress and suggested that the incoming Democratic majority may prove easier to negotiate with than Republicans.
Speaking to reporters in the briefing room, Trump described Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House, as “streetwise” and “smart,” and also praised the current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, a striking change in tone toward two lawmakers with whom he has repeatedly clashed. Trump also said prominent Democrats had already reached out to him privately about making potential deals next year on health care and immigration.
The comments offered one of the clearest indications yet of how Trump intends to navigate a dramatically altered political landscape following the midterm elections, which delivered Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and left the President facing the prospect of two years of legislative gridlock, aggressive congressional investigations, and potentially another effort to impeach him.
Trump appeared eager to present himself as a potential negotiating partner, even as he emphasized that he would use his veto power to block legislation he opposed. He suggested that Democratic leaders might eventually conclude that reaching compromises with him would be more productive than repeatedly passing bills he would reject.
“If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too,” Trump said. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care.”
Trump declined to identify the Democrats who had contacted him, saying only that they were influential figures interested in discussing two of the most contentious domestic policy questions. “I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he said. “People that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me about two things in particular: healthcare, because we can do something with healthcare together. Maybe easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation.”
It was not immediately clear whom Trump had spoken with or whether substantive negotiations had begun. Jeffries said earlier this month that he had not spoken with the President since the election.
Still, Trump’s remarks came as Democrats have begun assembling a legislative agenda that will test whether their sweeping electoral victory can translate into tangible policy achievements with a Republican president in the White House.
Health care, in particular, has emerged as a potential area of overlap, though significant disagreements remain over how far the federal government should go in expanding coverage and how to pay for it.
Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take power in January, has proposed a four-year transition toward Medicare for All. His plan would begin by lowering the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expanding benefits to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guaranteeing health coverage for children through age 18.
Jeffries has also indicated a willingness to pursue some of those priorities. This week, he said Democrats were preparing proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age, expand benefits and ensure health coverage for children. He has pledged to move quickly to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republican control.
Sanders has said that Trump might be more receptive than many Republicans assume. "Trump may be crazy, but he's not stupid, and he is a good politician,” Sanders said in a podcast posted to his YouTube page. “If we were to pass something that guaranteed healthcare to all people, that was enormously popular, and Trump says, 'I'm vetoing it.' Not a smart political move.”
Sanders added: "He may say, 'Well, I don't like this or that, let's sit down and negotiate it, but maybe I will sign something.' I think that's a possibility on a lot of legislation, because Trump has no ideology."
Whether Trump would embrace any of those proposals remains uncertain. Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would carry substantial federal costs, and the President has offered no specific commitments to expanding Medicare or reversing Medicaid reductions. But his suggestion that an agreement with Democrats might be easier than advancing legislation through budget reconciliation, a procedure that allows certain measures to bypass the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold, raised the possibility of a bipartisan alternative.
“Can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want,” Trump said. “We could end up with great health care in our country.”
Immigration presents a more complicated opening, particularly given Trump's decision after the election to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, to White House chief of staff. Jeffries denounced Miller as a “dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist,” underscoring the gulf between the Democratic leader and the administration.
Yet Trump has said that his administration's aggressive enforcement policies may have contributed to Republicans' devastating election losses. In a recent interview with 60 Minutes , Trump conceded that deporting immigrants who had lived and worked in the United States for years may have alienated voters who otherwise supported his border security agenda. “I think it might be too tough,” Trump said of his deportation policies. “That hurt me.”
He has suggested that a deal with Democrats could protect certain longtime residents who had committed no crimes beyond entering the country illegally, while preserving his administration's ability to deport people convicted of serious offenses.
This week, Jeffries said the new House majority would move early next year to advance the American Dream and Promise Act, legislation that would provide a path to permanent legal residency for immigrants brought to the United States as children and certain people protected from deportation under Temporary Protected Status.
Trump's friendlier tone toward Jeffries on Friday stood in sharp contrast to his history with the Democrat, whose relationship with the President has been marked by increasingly personal attacks. During a government funding dispute last year, Trump circulated an AI-generated video depicting Jeffries wearing a sombrero, which the Democratic leader denounced as racist and bigoted. Their exchanges grew even more caustic after Trump posted a video depicting former President Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama as apes, prompting Jeffries to call the president an “unhinged bottom feeder.”
Schumer, by contrast, has a longer personal history with Trump, dating to their years in New York politics. On Friday, Trump recalled giving Schumer what he described as his first political contribution, a $500 donation during an early campaign. “I always had a good relationship until I ran for office,” Trump said. “I was one of his backers.”
“I got richer and richer and richer, and he got more successful politically,” he added. “Who knew this was going to happen?”
Schumer is currently locked in a battle with Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for the Majority Leader role, which will be determined on Dec. 1. Jeffries, facing no challenger, was elected the Speaker-designate by House Democrats this week.

articles.title_orig: Experimental Drug Combination Cleared Tumors in Mice And Left Them Resistant to The Same Cancer
articles.title_zh: Experimental Drug Combination Cleared Tumors in Mice And Left Them Resistant to The Same Cancer
articles.content_orig:
Your immune system has a memory. It can recognize some microbes it has encountered before and respond quickly when they return. Could that memory also be strengthened against cancer?
A new study combining a cancer-killing drug with an experimental antibody produced evidence of that protection in mice. After their tumors disappeared, the animals resisted another injection of the same cancer cells weeks later, without further treatment.
Researchers at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, a US biotechnology company, wanted to strengthen cancer treatment by helping the immune system join the attack.
One part of the first combination was an established cancer drug. Sold as Enhertu, trastuzumab deruxtecan consists of an antibody carrying a cell-killing payload. The antibody binds to a growth-related protein called HER2, helping deliver that payload to cells carrying the protein.
Enhertu is already used for certain breast, stomach, and other cancers, depending on the tumor's characteristics and previous treatments. The experimental antibody added in this study had a different job: supporting immune cells that attack tumors.
Those defenders include T cells, which can recognize and kill cancer cells. An effective response generally requires both recognition of a target and an additional activation signal.
The experimental antibody binds to two different targets. One part attaches to a protein on tumor cells, while the other engages an activation protein on T cells called CD28. This two-target design makes it a "bispecific" antibody.
The researchers tested the combinations in mice carrying engineered mouse breast or colorectal tumors. The animals expressed human CD28 and modified versions of selected treatment targets. For HER2 and another growth-related protein, EGFR, the exposed outer portions were human, while the membrane-spanning and inner portions remained mouse. Tumor cells were also engineered to display the relevant targets.
In the initial breast cancer tests, the cancer drug alone produced complete tumor responses in fewer than half the mice, even at the highest dose tested. Combined with the experimental antibody, it eliminated tumors in all nine mice receiving both treatments.
The researchers then asked whether protection would last. After mice had remained tumor-free for at least four weeks, the team injected the same breast cancer cells again. The animals rejected them without additional treatment.
Another comparison helped reveal what their immune systems remembered. A different colorectal tumor grew in the previously treated mice, even though its cells also carried HER2. That suggested the protection recognized other features of the original cancer beyond the shared protein.
Removing a cancer-killing group of T cells, known as CD8 T cells, completely abolished the initial combination's benefit, showing these cells were essential to its success.
The team also tested an experimental antibody targeting EGFR, already in early-stage (phase 1/2) human trials. Combined with Enhertu, it produced tumor rejection in about 75 percent of mice in a breast tumor model more resistant to Enhertu alone.
The same antibody also worked with the chemotherapy drug fluorouracil, or 5-FU, already used for colorectal and other cancers. Together, the treatments slowed colorectal tumor growth when either treatment alone had little effect.
This combination relied on both CD8 T cells and another cancer-killing population, called natural killer, or NK, cells. The treatment retained some activity when either population was absent. Its benefit disappeared entirely when both were missing.
To investigate the immune response against cancer , the researchers examined cells inside tumors and analyzed gene activity. The combinations increased active T cells while preserving less mature cells that could support future responses.
They also increased the diversity of the receptors T cells use to recognize targets, potentially helping them recognize more features of the cancer.
Enhertu increased and activated dendritic cells, which show pieces of tumor material to T cells. In mice genetically engineered to lack a particular group of these cells, the Enhertu–antibody combination completely lost its effectiveness.
The chemotherapy drug worked differently. It shifted other immune cells toward supporting an attack and reduced populations that suppress it.
Some combinations remained effective with lower drug doses or less frequent chemotherapy, potentially reducing treatment burden if confirmed in patients.
The mouse models cannot reproduce the full range of side effects people may experience, including damage to the lungs, gut, heart, and skin. Effectiveness and safety in humans require further evaluation.
Regeneron funded the research. All authors are current or former employees, and provisional patent applications related to the work have been filed.
The research has been published in Nature Communications .

articles.title_orig: Russia attacks Zelensky's hometown, Ukraine reaffirms wish to join NATO
articles.title_zh: Russia attacks Zelensky's hometown, Ukraine reaffirms wish to join NATO
articles.content_orig:
A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed Friday night in a Russian “triple-tap” strike on the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih , according to local authorities.
In the attack on the home city of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, ballistic missiles hit a restaurant parking lot, then jet-powered drones struck rescue workers responding, city mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said. A third drone strike hit the location for a short time later.
This latest Russian assault comes after a busy week of diplomacy, including an unprecedented meeting between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Trump described Putin as a “friend” when they met – but in a CNN interview after, Zelensky said “for us, he is a killer.”
Nearly 60 others including rescuers and police officers were injured in the initial strike and follow-up attacks, Vilkul said.
He described the events as a “tragic evening and a tragic night for our city,” adding that the attack occurred “in the city center, near a popular restaurant, on Children’s Day.” In Ukraine, Children’s Day falls on November 20 and serves as a reminder of the need to protect children’s rights and advocate for their safety.
Dramatic footage from authorities showed people moving away from debris strewn across the street, only to scramble for cover as the sound of another incoming strike rang out.
Of those wounded, 28 remain hospitalized, including a three-year-old girl. Five of the 28 are in intensive care.
“Doctors are doing everything necessary to save their lives. Our condolences go out to the families and loved ones of those who died… We pray for the swiftest possible recovery of the injured , ” the mayor said.
Local broadcasting outlet Rudana named the seven-year-old boy who was killed in the Russian attack as Tikhon, describing him as kind, quick-witted and talented.
The boy’s family did not live in Kryvyi Rih, which is Zelensky’s hometown, but had been in the central Ukrainian city on business and decided to stop by their favorite restaurant, the outlet reported.
“We didn’t live here because it’s dangerous… but danger caught up with us,” the boy’s mother, Olena, told the outlet. According to the report, two of Olena’s other sons are in intensive care following the strike.
Zelensky said the attack on Friday night hit an ordinary civilian area of the city. “There are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been,” he said.
“Cities and villages in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipro, Rivne, Chernihiv, Mykolaiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions were also hit. In the Sumy region, a railway station came under attack,” the Ukrainian leader added.
Trump held talks with Putin and Xi at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, a meeting which was followed by a large “Coalition of the Willing” gathering in Berlin, attended by European leaders as well as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
In a joint statement after the meeting, the group of key Ukrainian allies declared they were ready to join direct negotiations with Moscow, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Russia’s “maximalist demands are not realistic.”
Zelensky on Saturday described the three-way meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi as “very unsuccessful” for the Russian leader, who he said had failed in his goal of trying to recreate a Yalta-style conference at which Allied powers divided up the postwar world in 1945 .
“China did not let itself be drawn in. As for the United States, I don’t know what went on between them and Russia in their bilateral talks, but Ukraine was not discussed. Nothing was said publicly,” Zelensky said in audio messages shared with journalists.
“So, the plan to redraw the world’s borders didn’t work out… I think the summit was a major failure for Russia.”
CNN’s Victoria Butenko and Laura Sharman contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Thousands take to streets in Portugal, France and Spain over rising living costs
articles.title_zh: Thousands take to streets in Portugal, France and Spain over rising living costs
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing and cuts to public services, as students and workers demand action from their governments.
Demonstrators marched across France and Portugal on Saturday, following youth-led protests in several European countries on Friday.
The gatherings reflect overlapping concerns about economic insecurity, education and future opportunities, although their demands and scale differ considerably between countries.
In France, the Ministry of Interior said 82,500 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, including 21,500 in Paris, down from 106,000 the previous weekend. Organisers estimated a higher turnout of 150,000.
About 70,000 members of the security forces were deployed across France to deter disorder. However, the Reuters news agency reported sporadic acts of violence, including in the southern city of Marseille.
Video also showed French police in riot gear charging at protesters in Paris in the evening. Loud bangs rang out amid smoke, fireworks and a burning car. Some protesters could be seen throwing objects towards police.
The protests, now in their sixth consecutive weekend, began in September with students demanding better schools, before expanding to include trade unions and the Yellow Vests, a movement that emerged in 2018 over rising fuel prices and living costs.
Demonstrators have also criticised police violence and a new law strengthening protections for officers who use firearms.
In Portugal, thousands marched through Lisbon despite heavy rain, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and relief from rising prices.
The demonstration was organised by CGTP, the country’s largest trade union federation, which also demanded higher pensions and cheaper essential goods.
Portugal’s housing pressures have intensified as property prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 percent below the European Union average, according to the EU’s statistics agency, Eurostat.
The weekend’s demonstrations followed Friday’s youth protests in Germany and Sweden.
About 4,000 people gathered in Berlin, while police in Helsinki reported roughly 200 participants at a Saturday march organised by left-wing and student groups.
Organisers of an international youth strike said demonstrations were planned in at least 25 countries, with demands ranging from greater education funding and climate action to opposition to compulsory military service.
In Germany, the youth campaign Gen Z regelt, meaning “Generation Z takes charge”, announced demonstrations in 73 locations.
In Italy, a nationwide strike organised by the CGIL, one of the country’s main trade union confederations, disrupted transport, schools and some healthcare services on Friday.
Demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities, with union leader Maurizio Landini claiming more than one million participants nationwide.
While some protests were linked through the international youth initiative, others grew out of established national campaigns, bringing different groups onto the streets over concerns about living standards and government spending.
Separately, thousands protested in the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on Saturday over the death of a man at a psychiatric hospital.
Four medical technicians are under investigation on suspicion of aggravated murder.

articles.title_orig: EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October
articles.title_zh: EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October
articles.content_orig:
High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!
This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!
Adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!
This great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).
At this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.
The ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.
Looking at the best sellers in several size categories , the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.
Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.
Considering that 56% of the new SUVs launched this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).
Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.
Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:
A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000) . This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the new generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.
BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the new generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations . Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?
BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations , which was a 44% increase YoY and a new record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles currently having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.
Things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its new baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations , the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….
After the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s new land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.
Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?
As for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!
Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the new generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.
Still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6 , the new China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!
A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also new VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?
Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s new baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be said about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi S

articles.title_orig: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming in 2027
articles.title_zh: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The glasses, code-named N50, are said to be slimmer than Meta's 2nd Gen Ray-Ban smart glasses.
Apple is the best-performing Magnificent Seven stock in 2026, having risen over 31% already.
Retail sentiment for AAPL dropped to 'bearish' on Monday.
Apple, Inc. (AAPL) is working on a pair of AI smart glasses and will debut them at its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) in June next year, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in his "Power On" column on Sunday.
The device, code-named N50, is built around Siri and iPhone apps and will offer users capabilities like Uber or Lyft booking, food ordering and buying movie tickets, according to Bloomberg. The glasses will also deliver iPhone notifications and support calendars and reminders, and won't work with Android phones.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
The reported move will put Apple directly in competition with Meta Platforms (META), whose Ray-Ban branded smart glasses have dominated the market.
Bloomberg reported that Apple's prototypes are slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Ban glasses, with cameras set flush into the frames. The design may change, although the first version is described internally as "AirPods for your face."
Shipments will begin before the end of 2027. Although the software underpinning the smart glasses is running behind schedule, Apple is trying to ramp up the development and bring the glasses to market in 2027 alongside an ambitious lineup to help celebrate the iPhone's 20th anniversary.
The report comes as Apple shares hit a record Friday, rising more than 4% for the week. The gains came as investors shifted money into other technology and industrial stocks during a selloff in Nvidia shares following Jensen Huang's departure as CEO.
AAPL is the best-performing Magnificent Seven stock in 2026, having risen over 31% already.
Under new CEO John Ternus, Apple is releasing new products at a fast clip. It recently announced Touchscreen MacBook Pros, the HomeView smart-home device, and the famous iPhone Duo.
On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for AAPL shifted to 'bearish' from 'neutral' as of early Monday.
"$AAPL It's crazy how all of us were making fun of Apple at the beginning of the year because of AI and now it's pumping," said a trader.
Some were, however, growing cautious. "$AAPL as I said on Friday, the chart is just starting to look like it's potentially time to start building a short position. 360 is guards the move higher. 355 lower. Chop between there is gonna burn both sides," said a second trader.

articles.title_orig: Teens want to play ‘Grand Theft Auto.’ Parents have a decision to make.
articles.title_zh: Teens want to play ‘Grand Theft Auto.’ Parents have a decision to make.
articles.content_orig:
A school concerned about pupils not coming in on the day the highly-anticipated GTA VI video game is released has offered young people prizes for turning up for classes.
Belfast Boys' Model school issued letters to parents, saying that the release of the game on Thursday coincided with GCSE maths exams.
The school said that "activities such as playing Grand Theft Auto can wait until the weekend".
On Monday, the school added that pupils who attended school on both Thursday and Friday would be entered into a draw for a £70 gift card for either PlayStation or Xbox.
In a letter issued to parents, reported by The Nolan Show , the school reminded "all parents and carers of the importance of ensuring that students attend school on Thursday 19th November".
It also said that "all Year 11 students and some Year 12 students" would be sitting a GCSE maths exam on Thursday, the same day the game comes out.
"Good attendance is one of the strongest indicators of academic success," the letter added.
Mary Montgomery, who is principal of the school, said "the primary focus" of her letter was Thursday's Mathematics examination and "encouraging our boys to be in school and ready to achieve their best".
"The results at GCSE have been fantastic in recent years and we want to continue that success for the boys," she said.
"It also highlighted the launch of GTA as something which might entice some boys to stay at home. However, the games vouchers were a pupil-led incentive."
Montgomery added: "They had said 'oh miss, you know GTA is coming out on Thursday and could we get GTA as a prize' was initially what they asked for to which I said 'no, it's an 18'."
GTA VI is released on Thursday, 13 years after the previous edition and with an estimated development cost of more $1bn (£866m) and is rated PEGI 18, meaning the game is for adults aged 18 and over.
In 2013, the term 'GTA Flu' was coined in reference to the large number of sick days reportedly taken when GTA V was released.
On Monday, the school announced that all pupils in attendance on Thursday and Friday would be entered into a draw to win one of two £70 gift cards "for PlayStation/Xbox".
Anthony, a 15-year-old pupil at the school told BBC News NI he is "very excited" about the game.
He has already downloaded it and when it is released he is "going to play it a lot".
"I've been waiting a long time for this," he said.
"You can pre download it now, install it now and when the game comes out you can instantly play it."
Michael, who is 17, is also excited to play the new GTA game, adding he thinks the school's idea to incentivise attendance is a "really good one".
The idea for the draw, which came from the pupils, will mark International Men's Health Day and raise money for charity.
"This idea is a really good one because gaming and mental health coincide a lot with men as they can use gaming as escapism from personal problems such as school, work and exams," Michael said.
He added: "We think gaming can be used as a way to negate the problems and stress that arise from school, so we brought that idea for the vouchers to get more people into school."
He added that gaming can help the pupils "switch off and manage some of the stress around exams, which is important with GCSE modules this week".
Speaking to The Nolan Show, a former school principal Kathleen O'Hare said the decision to send the letter to parents was "very wise".
"The cult of this game is so large that parents will be put under extreme pressure at times," she said.
O'Hare added that it has been "proven" that missing a day of school "really does matter".
Pete Wray, a Ulster Unionist Party councillor who works with children, said "there is a sizable amount of young people that are in our education system and completely disengage".
"They take an odd day off, and once they've got one day off, they're anxious about going back because they know they're going to be behind, and that leads to more and more problems," he said.
Wray said he will be imploring young people not to miss school to play the game, but that he "completely understands how people can become engrossed in it".
Considered one of the most highly-anticipated video games in history, the game is the latest in the long-running Grand Theft Auto series.
The game series, which has attracted controversy in the past over its depiction of violence and crime, is also the most expensive game ever made, with estimates putting development costs at more than $1bn (£866m).
The previous game in the series, GTA 5, sold nearly 230 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of all time, which has generated billions of dollars in revenue for developer Rockstar.
GTA 6 will feature its first ever playable female protagonist in a 3D setting - Lucia - alongside her partner in life and crime, Jason, as a second playable character.
Like other GTA games before it, the sixth chapter is set in a fictional US state - this time in Leonida, which is Rockstar's version of Florida.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO signals ‘beginning of a gold rush’ for small businesses, biz tech CEO says
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO signals ‘beginning of a gold rush’ for small businesses, biz tech CEO says
articles.content_orig:
Michael Rangel, who founded the small business financial technology platform Novo, explains that small businesses are only just beginning to adopt AI at a large scale and predicts an entrepreneurial gold rush after Anthropic's IPO.
Michael Rangel, founder of small business technology platform Novo, predicted that artificial intelligence tools will help usher in a "gold rush" for entrepreneurs and small businesses after a historic initial public offering for AI behemoth Anthropic.
"The solopreneur, so no employees: I think that is going to be a rocket ship. And I think that is actually one of the biggest things this country has been sleeping on is I truly believe we're going to be at the beginning of a gold rush here for the solopreneur," he told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
On Thursday, AI giant Anthropic officially filed its long-awaited initial public offering, opening with an initial valuation of $1.5 trillion.
TRUMP HOSTING ANTHROPIC CEO DARIO AMODEI FOR PRIVATE WHITE HOUSE DINNER
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks on the day Anthropic holds its initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City Nov. 19, 2026. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters / Reuters)
The company’s massive valuation and highly public offering signals a sea change in perception and adoption of the types of tools AI platforms offer for individuals and for businesses , Rangel explained.
Of Novo’s more than 250,000 small business clients, only one in 34 were using AI in 2023. Today that number has jumped to one in eight, he said.
"One in eight is a big jump. That means that they're moving fast. More people are adopting, more people are joining the herd, which is great. More people are chasing this productivity. They're trying to buy back their time," Rangel told Fox News Digital.
OPENAI CO-FOUNDER WARNS AI MODELS ARE BECOMING HARDER TO CONTROL AFTER ITS MODEL HACKED ANOTHER FIRM
"They're trying to do all of these things. But the flip side of that is that means there's still seven in eight businesses who have not. That is (an) opportunity for both Anthropic , the IPO, future prospects, growth, et cetera."
Those opportunities, Rangel revealed, often manifest in businesses he wouldn't have expected to be eager adopters of AI.
"Trucking, although it's analog, guess what AI can do? AI can't necessarily drive their trucks for them, at least not yet. They can completely rewire their back office," Rangel said.
Truckers with semi-trucks park in a rest area in Buttonwillow, Calif., June 26, 2026. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"How they think about accounting, payment, invoice management, all of those things — scheduling — all those things can be completely automated if they invest the time in getting it set up," he added.
Trucking, Rangel told Fox News Digital, was "the single segment that showed the biggest growth in AI adoption year over year. It doubled from 2025 to now; trucking, the segment, has doubled in AI penetration."
Restaurants, too, are now using AI tools to automate tasks in what Rangel calls "the back office," i.e. payroll, clerical work, healthcare and more.
Though Rangel claims to be "extremely bullish" on the future of AI for small business success, he says it will still take time to see widespread adoption.
FOX Business anchor Gerri Willis has the latest on the massive sell-off in the U.S. stock market amid a widespread artificial intelligence stock sell-off on 'Special Report.'
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
"I think you're still going to see this longer tail of analog businesses, analog industries who still need to leverage the technology and find the time to invest in their businesses so that they can leverage the opportunity and take their business to a new level," he said.
"And that's going to take a lot of time, like a long, long, time, for small businesses to change habits and systems."

articles.title_orig: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.title_zh: The sudden reversal in the stock market, and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators to discuss Iran negotiations
articles.content_orig:
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. ⁠The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and ⁠pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon's Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s latest flight of fancy involves potentially launching billions of dollars worth of cutting-edge AI chips into space.
Starting in late 2025 , the world’s richest man began pushing the ludicrous idea of launching AI data centers into orbit. Though humanity remains decades — if not centuries — away from cracking the physics on that fantastical concept, Musk has only become more enamored by the idea with the success of SpaceX’s debut on the public market.
Should he ever choose to pull the trigger on his orbital data centers, Musk would undoubtedly draw on the company’s incoming collection of Nvidia chips, financed by a massive loan from a cohort of the world’s most powerful banks.
The banks depending on those chips as collateral for SpaceX’s debt, however, are rightfully mortified.
New reporting by the Financial Times revealed that lenders backing a $43 billion SpaceX debt package — secured by the company’s cache of physical AI chips — have been trying to block any attempt by Musk and his board to greenlight a chip launch.
Given the fact that nobody has ever even attempted such a feat, SpaceX lenders would basically view any chips blasted into the stratosphere as lost, anonymous insiders told the FT . It’s not hard to see why: even if the chips do make it safely into orbit, physically repossessing them in the event that SpaceX defaults on its $43 billion loan would be a logistical nightmare.
While the contents of the final debt arrangement led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs are unknown to the public, the FT notes that an earlier proposal contained language allowing banks to legally challenge Musk’s orbital ambitions.
On a technical level, space-bound data centers are an absurdity at best. Each satellite would require enormous solar panel arrays to power low-gravity cooling pumps needed to dissipate heat, and if anything goes wrong, they’re a planet away from the nearest IT technician. That’s to say nothing of the regulatory hurdles around beaming that much data back and forth, or the impacts of solar radiation .

articles.title_orig: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.title_zh: Chainalysis reports 55% surge in China-linked stablecoin payments after US AI launches
articles.content_orig:
A survey of AI proxy services suggests stablecoins have become a key payment rail for Chinese users accessing restricted US models
Sat 21 Nov 2026 · 10:35 EST · 2 min read
Every time a major US AI lab ships a new frontier model, a shadow market on the other side of the Pacific starts paying up. In stablecoins.
That is the core finding of a new report from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. It found that payments from wallets suspected of links to China jumped 55% above baseline within three days of key US AI model releases.
Export controls were meant to keep advanced American AI out of reach. Instead, they appear to have created demand for a middleman economy, and crypto is helping settle the bill.
The report, published on November 21, 2026, describes a market where Chinese users reach restricted US frontier AI models through proxy or agent services. These services act as go-betweens, offering access that export controls would otherwise block.
Chainalysis surveyed 100 of these service providers. Of those, 40% accept payment in crypto, with stablecoins doing most of the work.
The timing pattern is what makes the data stand out. Activity from suspected China-linked wallets did not just drift upward over time. It spiked right after new US models dropped, which Chainalysis read as a sign of a coordinated rush to tap the latest capabilities.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
Chainalysis described an ecosystem with increasingly specialized roles.
Access suppliers provide the underlying connection to US models. Brokers connect buyers to that access. Payment processors handle the money side of the transaction.
Some of those payment players go a step further. According to the report, certain processors obscure stablecoin transactions by routing them through third-party channels, making the trail harder to follow.
The economics help explain why. Chainalysis noted that paying for proxy access is cheaper than training comparable models from scratch. Users can query US models and distill those capabilities into local systems, essentially learning from the output rather than building the foundation themselves.
The AI findings build on earlier Chainalysis work. A report released in October 2026 had already flagged a significant rise in peer-to-peer stablecoin transactions from China-linked wallets, despite domestic restrictions on crypto trading.
That October report recorded $104.1 billion in self-custodied stablecoin transfers from China-linked wallets. Those transfers came across 18.1 million transactions between July 2025 and June 2026.
Over the past year, the Chinese crypto ecosystem has been estimated at at least $176 billion. Peer-to-peer activity accounted for 59.1% of that total.

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.content_orig:
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI PS5 Streams/Captures Get DLSS 5 and Frame Generation on PC Through Veyra/Neural Screen, But Gameplay Still Runs at 30FPS (with More Latency)
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI PS5 Streams/Captures Get DLSS 5 and Frame Generation on PC Through Veyra/Neural Screen, But Gameplay Still Runs at 30FPS (with More Latency)
articles.content_orig:
We started playing Grand Theft Auto VI on a workbench with a processor AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card. A PlayStation 5 Pro console was connected to the computer via an AVerMedia Live Gamer ULTRA 2.1 GC553G2 external video capture card, and the game was run at 4K resolution with maximum graphics settings. Image output was organized using OBS Studio, and video recording was done using the NVIDIA App. To transform the image and achieve maximum smoothness, we enabled NVIDIA DLSS 5 (3D-Guided Neural Rendering) real-time generative neural rendering with the Natural profile and DLSS 4.5 frame generation in 6X mode using NeuralScreen v2.6.4.
In the opening scene in a correctional facility featuring protagonist Lucia Caminos, we directly compared standard console graphics and neural rendering. NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology works on top of the standard image to add photorealistic visual effects, radically changing the perception of the scene. With the neural network enabled, Lucia's face, skin texture, strands of hair, the folds of her prison uniform, and the soft light falling from the window all became realistically rendered. Simultaneously, six-times frame generation boosted performance to stable 262 and 280 FPS, with peaks of 286 FPS, ensuring incredibly smooth movement.
The RTX 5090 graphics card utilized 62% to 75% of its system capacity while running DLSS 5 generative neural rendering, maintaining a core clock of 2857 to 2917 MHz at temperatures ranging from 57° to 65°C and power consumption ranging from 305W to 368W. Without active neural rendering, with frame generation only, the GPU utilization dropped to 37% and 40%, while power consumption dropped to 189W and 214W. The system utilized approximately 5,3GB of video memory, and just over 12GB of RAM. AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D It ran stably at 5225 MHz, with temperatures ranging from 57° to 63° C and power consumption ranging from 41W to 48W, handling real-time streaming of Grand Theft Auto VI without issue.

articles.title_orig: Galaxy S27 Release Date: Early Software Reveals iPhone-Style Overhaul
articles.title_zh: Galaxy S27 Release Date: Early Software Reveals iPhone-Style Overhaul
articles.content_orig:
A new leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.
Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers , rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.
Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.
SamMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.
The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.
When this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That update is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.
What do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

articles.title_orig: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.title_zh: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.content_orig:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
after newsletter promotion
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.content_orig:
Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters .
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race .
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness .
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.
